21   Defendant Affiliated FM Insurance Company. ECF No. 192. For the reasons stated herein, the Court 
22   hereby DENIES the Motion for Leave to Amend and/or Supplement Answer.    
23     I.   Background                                                        
24          A.  Factual Background                                            
25        Plaintiff J-M Manufacturing, Inc. (“JM Eagle”) manufactures high grade, high performance 
26   plastic pipes. JM Eagle took out an “all risk” property insurance policy with Defendant Affiliated 
27   FM Insurance Company (“AFM”) for the period from November 1, 2016, to November 1, 2017 (the 
28

2   August 2017 due to damage caused by Hurricane Harvey.

5   Los Angeles, alleging claims for breach of contract, tortious breach of the implied covenant of good 
6   faith and fair dealing, and declaratory relief. ECF No. 1-1 (“Initial Complaint” or “Initial Compl.”) 
7   at 3. On June 26, 2019, AFM removed the action to federal court. ECF No. 1. On January 15, 2021,

    (emphasis added).                                                        
14                                                                            
         On March 12, 2022, AFM filed the operative Answer to the SAC. ECF No. 115 (“Answer”). 
15                                                                            
         On December 14, 2022, JM Eagle filed Motions in Limine, particularly one seeking to 
16                                                                            
    exclude evidence and argument regarding AFM’s fraud and misrepresentation affirmative defense. 
17                                                                            
    ECF No. 181 (“JME MIL 1”). On January 19, 2023, AFM filed the instant Motion for Leave to 
18                                                                            
    Amend and/or Supplement its Answer. ECF No. 192; 193 (“Mot.” or “Motion”). The Motion was 
19                                                                            
    fully briefed on February 16, 2023. ECF Nos. 196 (“Opp’n”), 197 (“Reply”). The Court deemed this 
20                                                                            
    matter appropriate for resolution without oral argument and took the Motion under submission. See 
21                                                                            
    ECF No. 201.                                                             
22                                                                            
         AFM’s Proposed Amended Answer adds, in relevant part, new factual allegations regarding 
23                                                                            
    AFM’s fraud and misrepresentation affirmative defense. ECF No. 194-2 (“Proposed Amended 
24                                                                            
    Answer”). In particular, the Proposed Amended Answer includes the following new allegations:  
25                                                                            
26        Misrepresentation regarding maintenance of financial records        
27            Chuck Clark, JM Eagle’s Vice President of Production, made the following 
         representation in his Declaration in Support of JM Eagle’s Motion for Summary 
28        Judgment:                                                           

                                     3                                       
Case 2:19-cv-05550-MEMF-SK   Document 202   Filed 02/27/23   Page 4 of 9   Page ID #:6732

             JM  Eagle  recognizes  company-wide  profits  and  losses  as  a  company 
1                                                                            
         headquartered  in  Los  Angeles  and  does  not  have  subsidiary  entities  located  at 
2        manufacturing facilities. Accordingly, JM Eagle does not maintain separate financial 
         records on a plant-by-plant or location-by-location basis. All financial records are 
3        maintained on a company-wide basis.                                 
4        Decl. of Chuck Clark, ¶ 10 [ECF No. 138-8, at Page ID #4760-61].     
5                                                                            
             This representation was knowingly false. JM Eagle previously represented that 
6        it had monthly income statements for its individual plants from 2015 through 2018 and, 
         in fact, had produced those monthly income statements by plant. In addition, JM Eagle 
7        admitted in a letter to AFM that its “January 11 claim submission details JM Eagle’s 
         losses by plant, which allows Affiliated FM to segregate . . . JM Eagle’s Supply Chain 
8        losses suffered at its other plants.” Furthermore, JM Eagle’s damages expert measured 
         the  Supply  Chain  loss  by  allocating  the  claimed  loss  to  18  different  JM  Eagle 
9                                                                            
         production facilities.                                              
10                                                                            
             JM  Eagle’s  misrepresentation  that  it  does  not  maintain  separate  financial 
11        records on a plant-by-plant or location-by-location basis and that financial records are 
         maintained on a company-wide basis was material in that it was made after the Court’s 
12        summary judgment ruling in an attempt to apply the $2.5 million sub-limit (and not the 
         $2 million Business Interruption sub-limit for all non-headquarters locations as found 
13        by the Court) to its Supply Chain claim.                            
14                                                                            
         Misrepresentation regarding “wind” as cause of damage               
15                                                                            
             JM Eagle represented in its First and Second Amended Complaints and in its 
16        Second Amended and Supplemental Proof of Loss signed under penalty of perjury that 
         all physical damage sustained at the Wharton facility from August 25 through August 
17        27, 2017, and all Business Interruption losses arising out of that damage, were not 
         caused by “Wind” as defined in the AFM Policy.                      
18                                                                            
             This representation was knowingly false. At a May 23, 2019 meeting between 
19                                                                            
         AFM and JM Eagle and their counsel at JM Eagle’s headquarters, JM Eagle’s counsel 
20        represented that:                                                   
21            a.  Most of the damage that has been claimed by JM Eagle was caused 
                by wind-driven rain and not by flood; and                    
22                                                                            
             b.  AFM should initiate the valuation process in order to calculate the 
23               wind deductible for a potential forthcoming wind claim.      
24                                                                            
             In its Complaint filed on May 28, 2019—nearly two years after Hurricane 
25        Harvey—JM Eagle admitted that:                                      
26            All physical damage sustained at the Wharton facility from August 25 through 
         August 27, 2017, and all Business Interruption losses arising out of that damage, were 
27        caused by "Wind" as defined in the Policy . . ..                    
28        (Compl., ¶ 29(c) [ECF No. 1-1, at Page ID # 13].) (Ex. 260)         

                                     4                                       
Case 2:19-cv-05550-MEMF-SK   Document 202   Filed 02/27/23   Page 5 of 9   Page ID #:6733

             Similarly, in its original Proof of Loss for the Wharton facility, signed under 
1                                                                            
         penalty of perjury and prepared on October 7, 2019 and its Amended Proof of Loss 
2        signed under penalty of perjury and dated September 28, 2020, JM Eagle represented 
         that “tornadic rain and wind” caused the nonflood damage at the Wharton facility.   
3                                                                            
             JM Eagle’s misrepresentation that all physical damage sustained at the Wharton 
4        facility from August 25 through August 27, 2017, and all Business Interruption losses 
         arising out of that damage, were not caused by "Wind" as defined in the AFM Policy 
5                                                                            
         was material in that it was made after the Court’s summary judgment ruling in an 
6        attempt to avoid application of the “Wind and Hail” deductible as found by the Court.   
7                                                                            
    Proposed Amended Answer at 13–15.                                        
8                                                                            
      II.  Applicable Law                                                    
9                                                                            
         Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 15(a), a party seeking to amend an Answer may do so 
10                                                                            
    once “as a matter of course” within 21 days after serving it. FED. R. CIV. P. 15(a)(1)(A). A party 
11                                                                            
    seeking to amend an Answer more than 21 days after serving it “may amend its pleading only with 
12                                                                            
    the opposing party’s written consent or the court’s leave. The court should freely give leave when 
13                                                                            
    justice so requires.” FED. R. CIV. P. 15(a)(2).                          
14                                                                            
         Once the district court has issued a CTO establishing the schedule of discovery, pretrial, and 
15                                                                            
    trial dates, Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 16 governs the standards for amending pleadings. 
16                                                                            
    Johnson v. Mammoth Recreations, Inc., 975 F.2d 604, 607–08 (9th Cir. 1992). Rule 16 provides in 
17                                                                            
    relevant part:                                                           
18                                                                            
         (b) [The district court] . . . shall, after consulting with the attorneys for the parties and 
19        any unrepresented parties, by a scheduling conference, . . . enter a scheduling order that 
         limits the time                                                     
20            (1) to join other parties and to amend the pleadings;           
             (2) to file and hear motions; and                               
21                                                                            
             (3) to complete discovery.                                      
22            . . .                                                           
         The order shall issue as soon as practicable but in no event more than 120 days after 
23        filing of the complaint. A schedule shall not be modified except by leave of ... [the 
         district court] upon a showing of good cause.1                      
24                                                                            
25                                                                            

26                                                                            
    1 The Court notes that orders entered before the final pretrial conference may be modified upon a showing of 
27                                                                            
    “good cause,” FED. R. CIV. P. 16(b), but orders “following a final pretrial conference shall be modified only 
28                                                                            
    to prevent manifest injustice.” FED. R. CIV. P. 16(e). Because the final pretrial conference has not yet 
    occurred, the Court considers this motion under the “good cause” standard. 

                                     5                                       
Case 2:19-cv-05550-MEMF-SK   Document 202   Filed 02/27/23   Page 6 of 9   Page ID #:6734

1   FED. R. CIV. P. 16. Under Rule 16, a district court may find “good cause” to amend the CTO “if [the 
2   CTO deadline] cannot reasonably be met despite the diligence of the party seeking the extension.” 
3   Johnson, 975 F.2d at 609 (quoting FED. R. CIV. P. 16 advisory committee’s notes (1983 
4   amendment)). “If the party seeking the modification ‘was not diligent, the inquiry should end’ and 
5   the motion to modify should not be granted.” Zivkovic v. Southern California Edison Co., 302 F.3d 
6   1080, 1087 (9th Cir. 2002) (quoting Johnson, 975 F.2d at 609). Moreover, Courts have held that 
7   carelessness may not be cited as a reason for modification and is not a basis upon which relief may 
8   be granted. See, e.g., Johnson, 975 F.2d at 609 (collecting cases).      
9        Because a motion for amending the CTO and amending a complaint may appear similar at 
10   first glance, courts have explicitly differentiated the evaluation of “good cause” under Rule 16 from 
11   the evaluation of the propriety of amendment under Federal Rules of Civil Procedure Rule 15. Id. at 
12   609. “Unlike Rule 15(a)’s liberal amendment policy, which focuses on the bad faith of the party 
13   seeking to interpose an amendment and the prejudice to the opposing party, Rule 16(b)’s ‘good 
14   cause’ standard primarily considers the diligence of the party seeking the amendment.” Id.   
15     III.  Discussion                                                       
16        Here, AFM requests permission to amend and/or supplement its Answer on the grounds that 
17   there has been no undue delay, there is no bad faith, amendment would not be futile, JM Eagle 
18   would not be prejudiced, no additional discovery is needed, and this is AFM’s first requested 
19   amendment. Mot. at 11–17. JM Eagle opposes the Motion, no “good cause” exists for AFM’s failure 
20   to diligently seek leave to amend, AFM unduly delayed in amending its answer, AFM’s delayed 
21   amendment would prejudice JM Eagle, and the proposed amendments would be futile. Opp’n at 4–7.  
22        Before the Court may grant leave for AFM to amend or supplement its Answer, the Court 
23   must first determine whether AFM has demonstrated “good cause” to justify modifying the CTO—
24   and, more specifically, the deadline to amend pleadings. Under the operative CTO and Federal Rule 
25   of Civil Procedure 15(a), the deadline for AFM to amend their pleadings or add parties without leave 
26   of the Court expired on March 4, 2022 (the first business day after the 21-day deadline lapsed). See 
27   January 2021 CTO (“Parties who wish to amend pleadings or to add parties shall comply with Rule 
28   15(a) . . . .”). Although the parties previously submitted joint stipulations regarding the various 

                                     6                                       
Case 2:19-cv-05550-MEMF-SK   Document 202   Filed 02/27/23   Page 7 of 9   Page ID #:6735

1   claims and the CTO was modified multiple times, the parties have never stipulated to or otherwise 
2   indicated the need for a continuance of the deadline to amend the pleadings. In determining whether 
3   “good cause” exists to modify the deadline to amend the pleadings, the Court must determine 
4   whether AFM made diligent attempts to amend the CTO.                     
5        AFM contends that “its affirmative defense is properly pled and no amendment is necessary,” 
6   but that “in an abundance of caution,” it seeks leave to amend and supplement its Answer to resolve 
7   issues raised in JME MIL 1. Mot. at 4. AFM asserts that the proposed amendments set forth detail 
8   regarding (1) “JM Eagle’s misrepresentation regarding the financial records maintained by JM 
9   Eagle, based on a declaration filed in June 2022” and (2) “JM Eagle’s misrepresentation regarding 
10   ‘wind’ as the cause of damage.” Id. It further notes that “[i]t was only after the Court issued several 
11   summary judgment rulings in AFM’s favor in July 2021 that JM Eagle changed course and adopted 
12   its current position regarding cause of damage at the JM Eagle Wharton facility. Id. at 4–9. 
13        AFM contends that it acted diligently, as it requested to leave to amend on January 19, 2023, 
14   after JM Eagle raised an objection to AFM’s existing defense on December 14, 2022. Mot. at 10. 
15        The Court finds that, by AFM’s own admission, the facts forming the basis for the new 
16   allegations was available to AFM as early as July 2021 (for the second alleged misrepresentation 
17   regarding cause of damage) and June 2022 (for the first alleged misrepresentation regarding the 
18   financial records maintained by JM Eagle). In July 2021, the Court issued a summary judgment 
19   ruling holding that the “Wind and Hail” deductible of over $2 million would apply to JM Eagle’s 
20   non-flood losses at the Wharton facility, which AFM alleges led JM Eagle to represent—allegedly 
21   falsely—that its non-flood damages and losses at the Wharton facility were caused by “vertical rain” 
22   and not solely “wind.” Mot. at 6. Moreover, in June 2022, an officer of JM Eagle represented that 
23   “JM Eagle does not maintain separate financial records on a plant-by-plant or location-by-location 
24   basis.” Id. Given that months have passed since AFM became privy to the information necessary for 
25   its amendment, AFM’s failure to file a Motion to Amend the CTO or for Leave to Amend or 
26   Supplement Answer over the past year and a half indicates a lack of diligence. 
27                                                                            
28                                                                            

                                     7                                       
Case 2:19-cv-05550-MEMF-SK   Document 202   Filed 02/27/23   Page 8 of 9   Page ID #:6736

1        For purposes of this motion, it is of no moment that JM Eagle only first raised potential 
2   deficiencies in AFM’s answer in December 2022.2  AFM does not assert that it ever identified these 
3   misrepresentations as the basis of this affirmative defense prior to December 2022. And AFM does 
4   not point to anything that would have put JM Eagle on notice—prior to December 2022—that AFM 
5   would seek to use these facts to support this defense.                   
6        Although AFM asserts that delay alone is not sufficient grounds to deny leave to amend, its 
7   analysis and the cases cited in support of its assertion are concerned primarily with FED. R. CIV. P.’s 
8   standards for determining when to grant leave to amend pleadings—not whether to grant leave to 
9   amend the CTO. See, e.g., Howey v. United States, 481 F.2d 1187, 1190–91 (9th Cir. 1973) (holding 
10   that it is abuse of discretion to deny leave to amend pleadings based on delay alone); DCD 
11   Programs, Ltd. v. Leighton, 833 F.2d 183, 186 (“[D]elay, by itself, is insufficient to justify denial of 
12   leave to amend [a pleading].”); United States v. Webb, 655 F.2d 977, 980 (9th Cir. 1981) (“[D]elay 
13   alone no matter how lengthy is an insufficient ground for denial of leave to amend [pleadings].”); 
14   Inteliclear, LLC v. ETC Glob. Holdings, Inc., 2021 WL 2370617, at * 4 (C.D. Cal. Feb. 2, 2021) 
15   (“As the Court has already determined a lack of prejudice, it declines to deny leave to amend [the 
16   complaint] solely because of delay.”). Indeed, the primary question when considering a request for 
17   leave to amend the CTO is whether good cause exists to do so and, in particular, whether the 
18   requesting party was diligent in seeking amendment. Johnson, 975 F.2d at 609; Zivkovic, 302 F.3d at 
19   1087.                                                                    
20        In light of the foregoing reasons, the Court concludes that AFM has failed to demonstrate 
21   good cause to justify a modification of the CTO. See FED. R. CIV. P. 16(b). Accordingly, the Court 
22   DECLINES to amend the CTO.                                               
23        Because the Court has declined to amend the CTO, the Court need not consider AFM’s 
24   Motion for Leave to Amend/Supplement the Answer. Because AFM’s “ability to amend his 
25                                                                            

26   2 Even assuming that AFM did not become aware of the potential deficiencies in its Answer until December 
    14, 2022, its actions still indicate a lack of diligence. The instant Motion was not filed until January 19, 
27                                                                            
    2023—over a month since JM Eagle filed its Motion in Limine 1 and nearly a month after the Court 
    continued the pending Final Pretrial Conference to April 16, 2023. Yet, AFM made no effort in that period to 
28                                                                            
    seek Leave to Amend the CTO or the Answer.                               

                                     8                                       
Case 2:19-cv-05550-MEMF-SK   Document 202   Filed 02/27/23   Page 9 of 9   Page ID #:6737

1   complaint [is] governed by Rule 16(b)” and it has not demonstrated “good cause,” the CTO will not 
2   be amended. Johnson, 975 F.2d at 608. Since the CTO’s deadline to file amended pleadings remains 
3   in place, the Motion for Leave to Amend/Supplement the Answer is therefore DENIED as untimely. 
4   U.S. Dominator, Inc. v. Factory Ship Robert E. Resoff, 768 F.2d 1099, 1104 (9th Cir. 1985) 
5   (concluding that because the parties never modified the CTO before the deadline had passed, the 
6   district court properly denied the motion to amend as untimely).         
7     IV.  Conclusion                                                        
8        For the foregoing reasons, the Court hereby ORDERS that the Motion for Leave to 
9   Amend/Supplement the Answer (ECF No. 192) is DENIED.                     
10                                                                            
11        IT IS SO ORDERED.                                                   
12

      II.  Applicable Law                                                    
9                                                                            
         Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 15(a), a party seeking to amend an Answer may do so 
10                                                                            
    once “as a matter of course” within 21 days after serving it. FED. R. CIV. P. 15(a)(1)(A). A party 
11                                                                            
    seeking to amend an Answer more than 21 days after serving it “may amend its pleading only with 
12                                                                            
    the opposing party’s written consent or the court’s leave. The court should freely give leave when 
13                                                                            
    justice so requires.” FED. R. CIV. P. 15(a)(2).                          
14                                                                            
         Once the district court has issued a CTO establishing the schedule of discovery, pretrial, and 
15                                                                            
    trial dates, Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 16 governs the standards for amending pleadings. 
16                                                                            
    Johnson v. Mammoth Recreations, Inc.,
975 F.2d 604
, 607–08 (9th Cir. 1992). Rule 16 provides in 
17                                                                            
    relevant part:                                                           
18                                                                            
         (b) [The district court] . . . shall, after consulting with the attorneys for the parties and 
19        any unrepresented parties, by a scheduling conference, . . . enter a scheduling order that 
         limits the time                                                     
20            (1) to join other parties and to amend the pleadings;           
             (2) to file and hear motions; and                               
21                                                                            
             (3) to complete discovery.                                      
22            . . .                                                           
         The order shall issue as soon as practicable but in no event more than 120 days after 
23        filing of the complaint. A schedule shall not be modified except by leave of ... [the 
         district court] upon a showing of good cause.1                      
24                                                                            
25                                                                            

26

27

28                                                                            
    to prevent manifest injustice.” FED. R. CIV. P. 16(e). Because the final pretrial conference has not yet 
    occurred, the Court considers this motion under the “good cause” standard.

7   carelessness may not be cited as a reason for modification and is not a basis upon which relief may

975 F.2d at 609
 (collecting cases).      
9        Because a motion for amending the CTO and amending a complaint may appear similar at 
10   first glance, courts have explicitly differentiated the evaluation of “good cause” under Rule 16 from 
11   the evaluation of the propriety of amendment under Federal Rules of Civil Procedure Rule 15.
Id.
 at 
12   609. “Unlike Rule 15(a)’s liberal amendment policy, which focuses on the bad faith of the party 
13   seeking to interpose an amendment and the prejudice to the opposing party, Rule 16(b)’s ‘good 
14   cause’ standard primarily considers the diligence of the party seeking the amendment.”
Id.
   
15     III.  Discussion                                                       
16        Here, AFM requests permission to amend and/or supplement its Answer on the grounds that 
17   there has been no undue delay, there is no bad faith, amendment would not be futile, JM Eagle 
18   would not be prejudiced, no additional discovery is needed, and this is AFM’s first requested 
19   amendment. Mot. at 11–17. JM Eagle opposes the Motion, no “good cause” exists for AFM’s failure 
20   to diligently seek leave to amend, AFM unduly delayed in amending its answer, AFM’s delayed 
21   amendment would prejudice JM Eagle, and the proposed amendments would be futile. Opp’n at 4–7.  
22        Before the Court may grant leave for AFM to amend or supplement its Answer, the Court 
23   must first determine whether AFM has demonstrated “good cause” to justify modifying the CTO—
24   and, more specifically, the deadline to amend pleadings. Under the operative CTO and Federal Rule 
25   of Civil Procedure 15(a), the deadline for AFM to amend their pleadings or add parties without leave 
26   of the Court expired on March 4, 2022 (the first business day after the 21-day deadline lapsed). See 
27   January 2021 CTO (“Parties who wish to amend pleadings or to add parties shall comply with Rule 
28   15(a) . . . .”). Although the parties previously submitted joint stipulations regarding the various

Id.
 It further notes that “[i]t was only after the Court issued several

 at 4–9. 
13        AFM contends that it acted diligently, as it requested to leave to amend on January 19, 2023,

21   falsely—that its non-flood damages and losses at the Wharton facility were caused by “vertical rain” 
22   and not solely “wind.” Mot. at 6. Moreover, in June 2022, an officer of JM Eagle represented that 
23   “JM Eagle does not maintain separate financial records on a plant-by-plant or location-by-location 
24   basis.”
Id.
 Given that months have passed since AFM became privy to the information necessary for

6        Although AFM asserts that delay alone is not sufficient grounds to deny leave to amend, its 
7   analysis and the cases cited in support of its assertion are concerned primarily with FED. R. CIV. P.’s 
8   standards for determining when to grant leave to amend pleadings—not whether to grant leave to 
9   amend the CTO. See, e.g., Howey v. United States,
481 F.2d 1187
, 1190–91 (9th Cir. 1973) (holding 
10   that it is abuse of discretion to deny leave to amend pleadings based on delay alone); DCD 
11   Programs, Ltd. v. Leighton,
833 F.2d 183, 186
 (“[D]elay, by itself, is insufficient to justify denial of 
12   leave to amend [a pleading].”); United States v. Webb,
655 F.2d 977, 980
 (9th Cir. 1981) (“[D]elay 
13   alone no matter how lengthy is an insufficient ground for denial of leave to amend [pleadings].”); 
14   Inteliclear, LLC v. ETC Glob. Holdings, Inc.,
2021 WL 2370617
, at * 4 (C.D. Cal. Feb. 2, 2021) 
15   (“As the Court has already determined a lack of prejudice, it declines to deny leave to amend [the 
16   complaint] solely because of delay.”). Indeed, the primary question when considering a request for 
17   leave to amend the CTO is whether good cause exists to do so and, in particular, whether the 
18   requesting party was diligent in seeking amendment. Johnson,
975 F.2d at 609
; Zivkovic, 302 F.3d at 
19   1087.                                                                    
20        In light of the foregoing reasons, the Court concludes that AFM has failed to demonstrate 
21   good cause to justify a modification of the CTO. See FED. R. CIV. P. 16(b). Accordingly, the Court
